newsitem.title: UK: Barclays drops again amid downgrade talk.
newsitem.headline: Barclays drops again amid downgrade talk.

text.p: Shares in Barclays Plc took another nosedive at midday on Tuesday as analysts downgraded the stock following a meeting with executives from the banking group to discuss 1996 earnings announced earlier.

Analysts at SBC Warburg cut the stock to "hold" from "buy," market sources said, and others were cautious on the outlook for the stock after Barclays posted a 13 percent rise in pre-tax profit to 2.36 billion stg, at the low end of expectations.
Even the group's announcement that it would return 500 million stg to shareholders failed to lift the stock, down 44p at 11.55-1/2 stg by 1235 GMT in volume of 15 million shares.

"The basic message is that there was disappointment about the headline profits and dividend, the mix of profits and the potential size of any buyback," said Michael Lever, analyst at HSBC James Capel.
"The figures were disappointing relative to expectations and everyone will be pulling their numbers back. I don't think they will make much more in 1997 than they did in 1996."

Market sources said estimates for Barclays pre-tax profit in 1997 were being trimmed by about 200 million stg but others pointed out that the reaction in the stock was mainly due to some overheated expectations.
"I do expect some downward pressure on estimates, maybe things got a bit too exuberant," said John Leonard, analyst at Salomon Brothers.

Leonard said he did not expect to make any major adjustment to his own forecasts, which were at the low end of expectations, though he said Barclays' headline figures had been flattered by factors including unusually low bad debt provisions.

Yet the Salomon analyst said he remained positive on Barclays and the sector as a whole because of the continuing favourable interest rate and inflation backdrop, against which bank stocks were among the best performers through 1996.
Others said the results showed continued strong growth at Barclays and were surprised at the share's reaction.
"The results looked fairly good to me," said one head of equity trading, "anyone making over 2 billion stg a year profits is doing well in my book."
